items.title: Kruk2/jasna
items.content:
Jasna restores mosaics in videos and images. It is free, has a simple app and a command line, and runs on your GPU.

  • Finds mosaics in a video and restores them. The rest of the picture is not touched.
  • Two restoration models: fast (free) and slow but more detailed (for supporters, NVIDIA only).
  • Restores only the parts you choose, with a preview, in the .
  • Works with VR180 videos and still images (SD 1.5, for supporters).
  • Lets you watch a video restored live in the , without making a file.
  • GTX 16-series / RTX 20-series or newer, with a recent driver (610+ on Windows, 580+ on Linux). GTX 10-series and older don't work.
  • Or Radeon RX 7000/9000 (experimental).
  • A folder on a local disk, with no Chinese, Japanese, accented or other non-English characters in its path.
  1. Download the release for your system and GPU.
  2. Unpack it into a folder with no Chinese, Japanese, accented or other non-English characters in the path.
  3. Start the app:
    • Windows: double-click .
    • Linux NVIDIA: run the file.
    • Linux AMD: run .
  4. Add a video, choose settings and click the button at the bottom.

On NVIDIA, Jasna first prepares the models for your exact GPU. This takes about , only once. Close other apps and don't use the PC during this time. When you update Jasna, copy the folder to the new version, so you don't wait again.

Every setting has a tooltip: move the mouse over the ⓘ icon. Out of GPU memory (VRAM)? Lower , for example from to . See Tuning.

  • App guide: the queue, presets, output names, the Video Player and activation.
  • Problem? Click at the bottom of the app, then to save a log file. Attach it when you ask for help.

Jasna is free. Your support pays for training new models, mostly GPU rental. Supporters get a License code for the supporter models:

: makes restored areas sharper.: experimental model for still images.
and , plus: much slower than BasicVSR++, but more detail. NVIDIA only. Includes future updates of this LTX model.

Supporters who gave $15 USD or more on or before 14 October 2026 get LTX for free.

  • Run LTX in on your PC. It is free and shows if your GPU can run LTX and how long it takes. The video is not restored. See What LTX needs.

License codes come from here:

Anyone else selling Jasna, codes or modified files is a scam: their keys don't work, and their files can run hidden code on your PC. Download Jasna only from GitHub.

  1. Support on one of the pages above. You get a .
  2. In Jasna, open , enter the License code and press .

One License code works on 3 PCs or cloud workspaces. After activation, Jasna works offline. Rented GPUs: see Cloud GPUs.

What counts as a new PC: on Windows, a new motherboard; on Linux, a fresh Linux install. Each uses one of your 3 slots. Reinstalling Windows or changing the GPU, disk or RAM does not: just activate again with the same License code. A few Windows PCs have no real motherboard ID; on those, a new system disk also counts as a new PC.

Have an email and key from Jasna 0.10? They no longer work. Get a new License code from where you bought it.

Almost everything runs on the GPU, from reading the video to saving it.

  1. the video on the GPU (NVDEC on NVIDIA, AMF on AMD).
  2. mosaics in each frame (default model ).
  3. each mosaic over time and group its frames into clips (up to frames). Clips end at scene cuts, so two different shots are never mixed.
  4. each clip as a 256x256 picture with BasicVSR++. Clips overlap a little, so there are no visible jumps between them.
  5. Optional (UNet 4x, RTX Super Res or Topaz TVAI) makes the restored picture bigger and sharper.
  6. the restored picture back into the original frame. Only the mosaic area changes.
  7. with the GPU encoder (NVENC on NVIDIA, AMF on AMD). Audio is copied (encoded again only if the output format can't hold it).

The first job is slow because the models for steps 2 and 4 (and UNet 4x, if used) are prepared for your exact GPU (NVIDIA only). The result is saved in and used again later. You can copy it to a newer Jasna version.

LTX works differently. It goes over the video in 4 passes: find mosaics, prepare, restore with a diffusion model, save. It is slower but can add more real detail. See Choosing models.

The command line can do most of what the app does (not the Video Player, LTX seed previews, mask suggestions or interactive image mode).

# One video
jasna --input input.mp4 --output output.mkv

# One image
jasna --input photo.png --output restored.png

# A whole folder
jasna --input input_folder --output output_folder

Time to restore a whole 3:22 video with BasicVSR++ on an RTX 5090 (Linux). Lower is better.

  • : Jasna is inspired by Lada and in some places based on it. The model used by Jasna was trained by ladaapp, the author of Lada.
  • : for the VR detection model and the detailed analysis of mosaic shapes and VR projection.

items.title: mlabonne/llm-course
items.content:
Course to get into Large Language Models (LLMs) with roadmaps and Colab notebooks.

The LLM course is divided into three parts:

  1. 🧩 is optional and covers fundamental knowledge about mathematics, Python, and neural networks.
  2. 🧑‍🔬 focuses on building the best possible LLMs using the latest techniques.
  3. 👷 focuses on creating LLM-based applications and deploying them.

Based on this course, I co-wrote the LLM Engineer's Handbook, a hands-on book that covers an end-to-end LLM application from design to deployment. The LLM course will always stay free, but you can support my work by purchasing this book.

For a more comprehensive version of this course, check out the DeepWiki.

A list of notebooks and articles I wrote about LLMs.

This section introduces essential knowledge about mathematics, Python, and neural networks. You might not want to start here but refer to it as needed.

This section of the course focuses on learning how to build the best possible LLMs using the latest techniques.

An in-depth knowledge of the Transformer architecture is not required, but it's important to understand the main steps of modern LLMs: converting text into numbers through tokenization, processing these tokens through layers including attention mechanisms, and finally generating new text through various sampling strategies.

  • : Understand the evolution from encoder-decoder Transformers to decoder-only architectures like GPT, which form the basis of modern LLMs. Focus on how these models process and generate text at a high level.
  • : Learn the principles of tokenization - how text is converted into numerical representations that LLMs can process. Explore different tokenization strategies and their impact on model performance and output quality.
  • : Master the core concepts of attention mechanisms, particularly self-attention and its variants. Understand how these mechanisms enable LLMs to process long-range dependencies and maintain context throughout sequences.
  • : Explore various text generation approaches and their tradeoffs. Compare deterministic methods like greedy search and beam search with probabilistic approaches like temperature sampling and nucleus sampling.
  • nanoGPT by Andrej Karpathy: A 2h-long YouTube video to reimplement GPT from scratch (for programmers). He also made a video about tokenization.
  • Decoding Strategies in LLMs by Maxime Labonne: Provide code and a visual introduction to the different decoding strategies to generate text.

Pre-training is a computationally intensive and expensive process. While it's not the focus of this course, it's important to have a solid understanding of how models are pre-trained, especially in terms of data and parameters. Pre-training can also be performed by hobbyists at a small scale with <1B models.

  • : Pre-training requires massive datasets (e.g., Llama 3.1 was trained on 15 trillion tokens) that need careful curation, cleaning, deduplication, and tokenization. Modern pre-training pipelines implement sophisticated filtering to remove low-quality or problematic content.
  • : Combine different parallelization strategies: data parallel (batch distribution), pipeline parallel (layer distribution), and tensor parallel (operation splitting). These strategies require optimized network communication and memory management across GPU clusters.
  • : Use adaptive learning rates with warm-up, gradient clipping, and normalization to prevent explosions, mixed-precision training for memory efficiency, and modern optimizers (AdamW, Lion) with tuned hyperparameters.
  • : Track key metrics (loss, gradients, GPU stats) using dashboards, implement targeted logging for distributed training issues, and set up performance profiling to identify bottlenecks in computation and communication across devices.
  • FineWeb by Penedo et al.: Article to recreate a large-scale dataset for LLM pretraining (15T), including FineWeb-Edu, a high-quality subset.
  • RedPajama v2 by Weber et al.: Another article and paper about a large-scale pre-training dataset with a lot of interesting quality filters.
  • nanotron by Hugging Face: Minimalistic LLM training codebase used to make SmolLM2.
  • Parallel training by Chenyan Xiong: Overview of optimization and parallelism techniques.
  • Distributed training by Duan et al.: A survey about efficient training of LLM on distributed architectures.
  • OLMo 2 by AI2: Open-source language model with model, data, training, and evaluation code.
  • LLM360 by LLM360: A framework for open-source LLMs with training and data preparation code, data, metrics, and models.

3. Post-Training Datasets

Post-training datasets have a precise structure with instructions and answers (supervised fine-tuning) or instructions and chosen/rejected answers (preference alignment). Conversational structures are a lot rarer than the raw text used for pre-training, which is why we often need to process seed data and refine it to improve the accuracy, diversity, and complexity of the samples. More information and examples are available in my repo 💾 LLM Datasets.

  • : Because of the conversational structure, post-training datasets are stored in a specific format like ShareGPT or OpenAI/HF. Then, these formats are mapped to a chat template like ChatML or Alpaca to produce the final samples that the model is trained on.
  • Synthetic data generation: Create instruction-response pairs based on seed data using frontier models like GPT-4o. This approach allows for flexible and scalable dataset creation with high-quality answers. Key considerations include designing diverse seed tasks and effective system prompts.
  • : Enhance existing samples using techniques like verified outputs (using unit tests or solvers), multiple answers with rejection sampling, Auto-Evol, Chain-of-Thought, Branch-Solve-Merge, personas, etc.
  • : Traditional techniques involve rule-based filtering, removing duplicates or near-duplicates (with MinHash or embeddings), and n-gram decontamination. Reward models and judge LLMs complement this step with fine-grained and customizable quality control.
  • Synthetic Data Generator by Argilla: Beginner-friendly way of building datasets using natural language in a Hugging Face space.
  • LLM Datasets by Maxime Labonne: Curated list of datasets and tools for post-training.
  • NeMo-Curator by Nvidia: Dataset preparation and curation framework for pre- and post-training data.
  • Distilabel by Argilla: Framework to generate synthetic data. It also includes interesting reproductions of papers like UltraFeedback.
  • Semhash by MinishLab: Minimalistic library for near-deduplication and decontamination with a distilled embedding model.
  • Chat Template by Hugging Face: Hugging Face's documentation about chat templates.

4. Supervised Fine-Tuning

SFT turns base models into helpful assistants, capable of answering questions and following instructions. During this process, they learn how to structure answers and reactivate a subset of knowledge learned during pre-training. Instilling new knowledge is possible but superficial: it cannot be used to learn a completely new language. Always prioritize data quality over parameter optimization.

  • : Full fine-tuning updates all model parameters but requires significant compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques like LoRA and QLoRA reduce memory requirements by training a small number of adapter parameters while keeping base weights frozen. QLoRA combines 4-bit quantization with LoRA to reduce VRAM usage. These techniques are all implemented in the most popular fine-tuning frameworks: TRL, Unsloth, and Axolotl.
  • : Key parameters include learning rate with schedulers, batch size, gradient accumulation, number of epochs, optimizer (like 8-bit AdamW), weight decay for regularization, and warmup steps for training stability. LoRA also adds three parameters: rank (typically 16-128), alpha (1-2x rank), and target modules.
  • : Scale training across multiple GPUs using DeepSpeed or FSDP. DeepSpeed provides three ZeRO optimization stages with increasing levels of memory efficiency through state partitioning. Both methods support gradient checkpointing for memory efficiency.
  • : Track training metrics including loss curves, learning rate schedules, and gradient norms. Monitor for common issues like loss spikes, gradient explosions, or performance degradation.
  • Axolotl - Documentation by Wing Lian: Lots of interesting information related to distributed training and dataset formats.
  • Mastering LLMs by Hamel Husain: Collection of educational resources about fine-tuning (but also RAG, evaluation, applications, and prompt engineering).
  • LoRA insights by Sebastian Raschka: Practical insights about LoRA and how to select the best parameters.

Preference alignment is a second stage in the post-training pipeline, focused on aligning generated answers with human preferences. This stage was designed to tune the tone of LLMs and reduce toxicity and hallucinations. However, it has become increasingly important to also boost their performance and improve their usefulness. Unlike SFT, there are many preference alignment algorithms. Here, we'll focus on the three most important ones: DPO, GRPO, and PPO.

  • : For each prompt, use the trained model to generate multiple responses, and score them to infer chosen/rejected answers. This creates on-policy data, where both responses come from the model being trained, improving alignment stability.
  • Directly optimizes the policy to maximize the likelihood of chosen responses over rejected ones. It doesn't require reward modeling, which makes it more computationally efficient than RL techniques but slightly worse in terms of quality. Great for creating chat models.
  • : Train a reward model with human feedback to predict metrics like human preferences. It can leverage frameworks like TRL, verl, and OpenRLHF for scalable training.
  • : RL techniques like GRPO and PPO iteratively update a policy to maximize rewards while staying close to the initial behavior. They can use a reward model or reward functions to score responses. They tend to be computationally expensive and require careful tuning of hyperparameters, including learning rate, batch size, and clip range. Ideal for creating reasoning models.

Reliably evaluating LLMs is a complex but essential task guiding data generation and training. It provides invaluable feedback about areas of improvement, which can be leveraged to modify the data mixture, quality, and training parameters. However, it's always good to remember Goodhart's law: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."

  • : Evaluate models on specific tasks using curated datasets and metrics, like MMLU. It works well for concrete tasks but struggles with abstract and creative capabilities. It is also prone to data contamination.
  • : It involves humans prompting models and grading responses. Methods range from vibe checks to systematic annotations with specific guidelines and large-scale community voting (arena). It is more suited for subjective tasks and less reliable for factual accuracy.
  • : Use judge and reward models to evaluate model outputs. It highly correlates with human preferences but suffers from bias toward their own outputs and inconsistent scoring.
  • : Analyze error patterns to identify specific weaknesses, such as limitations in following complex instructions, lack of specific knowledge, or susceptibility to adversarial prompts. This can be improved with better data generation and training parameters.
  • Open LLM Leaderboard by Hugging Face: Main leaderboard to compare LLMs in an open and reproducible way (automated benchmarks).
  • Lighteval by Hugging Face: Alternative evaluation framework that also includes model-based evaluations.
  • Chatbot Arena by LMSYS: Elo rating of general-purpose LLMs, based on comparisons made by humans (human evaluation).

Quantization is the process of converting the parameters and activations of a model to a lower precision. For example, weights stored using 16 bits can be converted into a 4-bit representation. This technique has become increasingly important to reduce the computational and memory costs associated with LLMs.

  • : Learn the different levels of precision (FP32, FP16, INT8, etc.) and how to perform naïve quantization with absmax and zero-point techniques.
  • : Originally designed to run on CPUs, llama.cpp and the GGUF format have become the most popular tools to run LLMs on consumer-grade hardware. It supports storing special tokens, vocabulary, and metadata in a single file.
  • : Techniques like GPTQ/EXL2 and AWQ introduce layer-by-layer calibration that retains performance at extremely low bitwidths. They reduce catastrophic outliers using dynamic scaling, selectively skipping or re-centering the heaviest parameters.
  • : New quantization-friendly transformations (SmoothQuant) and compiler-based optimizations (ZeroQuant) help mitigate outliers before quantization. They also reduce hardware overhead by fusing certain ops and optimizing dataflow.

Here are notable topics that didn't fit into other categories. Some are established techniques (model merging, multimodal), but others are more experimental (interpretability, test-time compute scaling) and the focus of numerous research papers.

  • : Merging trained models has become a popular way of creating performant models without any fine-tuning. The popular mergekit library implements the most popular merging methods, like SLERP, DARE, and TIES.
  • : These models (like CLIP, Stable Diffusion, or LLaVA) process multiple types of inputs (text, images, audio, etc.) with a unified embedding space, which unlocks powerful applications like text-to-image.
  • : Mechanistic interpretability techniques like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have made remarkable progress to provide insights about the inner workings of LLMs. This has also been applied with techniques such as abliteration, which allow you to modify the behavior of models without training.
  • : Reasoning models trained with RL techniques can be further improved by scaling the compute budget during test time. It can involve multiple calls, MCTS, or specialized models like a Process Reward Model (PRM). Iterative steps with precise scoring significantly improve performance for complex reasoning tasks.

This section of the course focuses on learning how to build LLM-powered applications that can be used in production, with a focus on augmenting models and deploying them.

Running LLMs can be difficult due to high hardware requirements. Depending on your use case, you might want to simply consume a model through an API (like GPT-4) or run it locally. In any case, additional prompting and guidance techniques can improve and constrain the output for your applications.

  • : Common techniques include zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, chain of thought, and ReAct. They work better with bigger models, but can be adapted to smaller ones.
  • : Many tasks require a structured output, like a strict template or a JSON format. Libraries like Outlines can be used to guide the generation and respect a given structure. Some APIs also support structured output generation natively using JSON schemas.

2. Building a Vector Storage

Creating a vector storage is the first step to building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline. Documents are loaded, split, and relevant chunks are used to produce vector representations (embeddings) that are stored for future use during inference.

  • : Document loaders are convenient wrappers that can handle many formats: PDF, JSON, HTML, Markdown, etc. They can also directly retrieve data from some databases and APIs (GitHub, Reddit, Google Drive, etc.).
  • : Text splitters break down documents into smaller, semantically meaningful chunks. Instead of splitting text after characters, it's often better to split by header or recursively, with some additional metadata.
  • : Embedding models convert text into vector representations. Picking task-specific models significantly improves performance for semantic search and RAG.
  • : Vector databases (like Chroma, Pinecone, Milvus, FAISS, Annoy, etc.) are designed to store embedding vectors. They enable efficient retrieval of data that is 'most similar' to a query based on vector similarity.

3. Retrieval Augmented Generation

With RAG, LLMs retrieve contextual documents from a database to improve the accuracy of their answers. RAG is a popular way of augmenting the model's knowledge without any fine-tuning.

  • : Orchestrators like LangChain and LlamaIndex are popular frameworks to connect your LLMs with tools and databases. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) introduces a new standard to pass data and context to models across providers.
  • : Query rewriters and generative retrievers like CoRAG and HyDE enhance search by transforming user queries. Multi-vector and hybrid retrieval methods combine embeddings with keyword signals to improve recall and precision.
  • : To remember previous instructions and answers, LLMs and chatbots like ChatGPT add this history to their context window. This buffer can be improved with summarization (e.g., using a smaller LLM), a vector store + RAG, etc.
  • : We need to evaluate both the document retrieval (context precision and recall) and the generation stages (faithfulness and answer relevancy). It can be simplified with tools Ragas and DeepEval (assessing quality).

Real-life applications can require complex pipelines, including SQL or graph databases, as well as automatically selecting relevant tools and APIs. These advanced techniques can improve a baseline solution and provide additional features.

  • : Structured data stored in traditional databases requires a specific query language like SQL, Cypher, metadata, etc. We can directly translate the user instruction into a query to access the data with query construction.
  • : Agents augment LLMs by automatically selecting the most relevant tools to provide an answer. These tools can be as simple as using Google or Wikipedia, or more complex, like a Python interpreter or Jira.
  • : Final step that processes the inputs that are fed to the LLM. It enhances the relevance and diversity of documents retrieved with re-ranking, RAG-fusion, and classification.
  • : Frameworks like DSPy allow you to optimize prompts and weights based on automated evaluations in a programmatic way.

An LLM agent can autonomously perform tasks by taking actions based on reasoning about its environment, typically through the use of tools or functions to interact with external systems.

  • : Agents operate using thoughts (internal reasoning to decide what to do next), action (executing tasks, often by interacting with external tools), and observation (analyzing feedback or results to refine the next step).
  • : Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the industry standard for connecting agents to external tools and data sources with MCP servers and clients. More recently, Agent2Agent (A2A) tries to standardize a common language for agent interoperability.
  • : Agent development can be streamlined using different frameworks like LangGraph (design and visualization of workflows) LlamaIndex (data-augmented agents with RAG), or custom solutions. More experimental frameworks include collaboration between different agents, such as CrewAI (role-based team workflows) and AutoGen (conversation-driven multi-agent systems).
  • Agents Course: Popular course about AI agents made by Hugging Face.
  • LangGraph: Overview of how to build AI agents with LangGraph.

6. Inference optimization

Text generation is a costly process that requires expensive hardware. In addition to quantization, various techniques have been proposed to maximize throughput and reduce inference costs.

  • : Optimization of the attention mechanism to transform its complexity from quadratic to linear, speeding up both training and inference.
  • : Use a small model to produce drafts that are then reviewed by a larger model to speed up text generation. EAGLE-3 is a particularly popular solution.
  • GPU Inference by Hugging Face: Explain how to optimize inference on GPUs.
  • LLM Inference by Databricks: Best practices for how to optimize LLM inference in production.
  • Optimizing LLMs for Speed and Memory by Hugging Face: Explain three main techniques to optimize speed and memory, namely quantization, Flash Attention, and architectural innovations.
  • Assisted Generation by Hugging Face: HF's version of speculative decoding. It's an interesting blog post about how it works with code to implement it.
  • EAGLE-3 paper: Introduces EAGLE-3 and reports speedups up to 6.5×.
  • Speculators: Library made by vLLM for building, evaluating, and storing speculative decoding algorithms (e.g., EAGLE-3) for LLM inference.

Deploying LLMs at scale is an engineering feat that can require multiple clusters of GPUs. In other scenarios, demos and local apps can be achieved with much lower complexity.

  • : Privacy is an important advantage that open-source LLMs have over private ones. Local LLM servers (LM Studio, Ollama, oobabooga, kobold.cpp, etc.) capitalize on this advantage to power local apps.
  • : Frameworks like Gradio and Streamlit are helpful to prototype applications and share demos. You can also easily host them online, for example, using Hugging Face Spaces.
  • : Deploying LLMs at scale requires cloud (see also SkyPilot) or on-prem infrastructure and often leverages optimized text generation frameworks like TGI, vLLM, etc.
  • : In constrained environments, high-performance frameworks like MLC LLM and mnn-llm can deploy LLM in web browsers, Android, and iOS.

In addition to traditional security problems associated with software, LLMs have unique weaknesses due to the way they are trained and prompted.

  • : Different techniques related to prompt engineering, including prompt injection (additional instruction to hijack the model's answer), data/prompt leaking (retrieve its original data/prompt), and jailbreaking (craft prompts to bypass safety features).
  • : Attack vectors can target the training data itself, by poisoning the training data (e.g., with false information) or creating backdoors (secret triggers to change the model's behavior during inference).
  • : The best way to protect your LLM applications is to test them against these vulnerabilities (e.g., using red teaming and checks like garak) and observe them in production (with a framework like langfuse).

This roadmap was inspired by the excellent DevOps Roadmap from Milan Milanović and Romano Roth.

  • Thomas Thelen for motivating me to create a roadmap
  • André Frade for his input and review of the first draft
  • Dino Dunn for providing resources about LLM security
  • Magdalena Kuhn for improving the "human evaluation" part
  • Odoverdose for suggesting 3Blue1Brown's video about Transformers
  • Everyone who contributed to the educational references in this course 😃

items.title: anomalyco/opencode
items.content:
The open source coding agent.

The open source AI coding agent.

# YOLO
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash

# Package managers
npm i -g @opencode/cli@latest      # or bun/pnpm/yarn
brew install anomalyco/tap/opencode-v2 # macOS and Linux (recommended, always up to date)
brew install opencode              # macOS and Linux (official brew formula, updated less)
sudo pacman -S opencode            # Arch Linux (Stable)
paru -S opencode-beta              # Arch Linux (Latest from AUR)
mise use -g opencode               # Any OS
nix run github:anomalyco/opencode  # Nix

Remove versions older than 0.1.x before installing.

opencode-desktop-mac-arm64.dmg
opencode-desktop-mac-x64.dmg
opencode-desktop-win-x64.exe
# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install --cask opencode-desktop

The install script respects the following priority order for the installation path:

  1. - Custom installation directory
  2. - XDG Base Directory Specification compliant path
  3. - Standard user binary directory (if it exists or can be created)
  4. - Default fallback
# Examples
OPENCODE_INSTALL_DIR=/usr/local/bin curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash
XDG_BIN_DIR=$HOME/.local/bin curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash

OpenCode includes two built-in agents you can switch between with the key.

  • - Default, full-access agent for development work
  • - Read-only agent for analysis and code exploration
    • Denies file edits by default
    • Asks permission before running bash commands
    • Ideal for exploring unfamiliar codebases or planning changes

Also included is a subagent for complex searches and multistep tasks. This is used internally and can be invoked using in messages.

If you're interested in contributing to OpenCode, please read our contributing docs before submitting a pull request.

If you are working on a project that's related to OpenCode and is using "opencode" as part of its name, for example "opencode-dashboard" or "opencode-mobile", please add a note to your README to clarify that it is not built by the OpenCode team and is not affiliated with us in any way.

items.title: debpalash/VoiceStudio
items.content:
VoiceStudio is the open-source, fully-local ElevenLabs alternative — voice cloning, voice design, video dubbing, dictation, transcription & audiobook creation in 646 languages.

Your voice. Your workflow.

items.title: akitaonrails/ai-memory
items.content:
Solution for long term memory for agent coding CLIs and to facilitate handoff between different agent vendors

Long-term memory for AI coding agents. Quit Claude Code mid-task, start OpenAI Codex in the same directory, continue without re-explaining the architecture, the failed approaches, or the open questions.

Your coding agent probably has a memory feature already. Claude Code takes its own notes, Cursor remembers some things, and every platform is adding more. They all have the same limits: the notes live on one machine, belong to one agent, and drop out of view when you switch tools or hand the work to a teammate.

ai-memory removes those limits.

  • It follows you across agents. More than twenty harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Grok, Devin, Kimi, Kiro, and others) feed one shared memory. Quit Claude Code mid-task, open Codex in the same directory, and the next agent picks up a handoff that says where you left off, what failed, and what is still open. Handoffs are a typed protocol: each one has an owner and is claimed exactly once.

  • It can carry the session, not just a summary. Start agents with : quit Claude Code, run , and Codex gets the shared workstream plus a private, temporary local projection of Claude's visible native history for exact details the bounded startup packet omitted. The remote server receives only the harness and session identity, never the local transcript path or body. Direct harness launches behave exactly as before.

  • It follows you across projects. A small profile of how you usually work (your package manager, test layout, architecture habits) reaches every new repository at session start, so you stop re-explaining yourself. It sits below each repository's rules file as a default. It is on by default for a single user, and on a shared server it is opt-in and private per person. See docs/cross-project-profile.md.

  • It follows you across machines. Memory lives in a server you run, on the same laptop, a homelab box, or anywhere else, so the project you left on the desktop is the project you resume on the laptop, with the same knowledge and the same open questions.

  • Point everyone at one server, and what one person's sessions learn, everyone's agents can retrieve. Knowledge is shared per project; personal handoffs stay personal. Multi-user auth, per-person attribution, and an audit log are built in and are not a paid tier.

  • Your memory is plain markdown. The source of truth is a git-backed wiki of ordinary files: it, open it in Obsidian, edit it by hand, it. The database is a derived index that can always be rebuilt from the files. There is no vector store to maintain and no content locked in a binary blob.

  • It captures the work itself, silently. Lifecycle hooks record what happened (prompts, tool calls, session boundaries), sanitize it at a typed privacy boundary before anything is stored, and the server consolidates it into readable pages. You do not have to ask it to remember anything. The default path uses : capture, search, and handoffs all work with no API key.

  • It ages memory without an LLM. Memory decays on a schedule you can tune per tier, and memory you use decays : opening a page, searching it, or reaching it through a link counts as use. When episodic notes go cold they can be compacted down to their durable facts (file paths, error codes, decisions) instead of dropped. Near-duplicates collapse into one, and likely contradictions get flagged, all with . Nothing is hard-deleted: the original stays in git and the version chain ( brings it back). Access-weighted retention is always on because it can only keep memory . The parts that rewrite or drop content (compaction, dedup, per-tier curves) stay off by default until you turn them on.

  • It can also "dream", if you let it. With an LLM configured, an opt-in background pass rewrites whole clusters of cold notes into single coherent pages while you are idle, and cancels as soon as you come back to work. It never deletes a source (the pre-merge versions stay reachable), it is off by default, and it has to pass a recall eval before it could become default behavior. Unless you ask for more, the zero-LLM path above is what runs.

  • It is honest about itself. It ships as one self-contained binary. Purge commands say exactly what "deleted" means. The write ceiling (~700/s) is measured, not guessed. An audit log records every mutation.

capture ──▶ consolidate ──▶ recall ──▶ handoff
 hooks        session-end      search     next agent,
 observe      summaries as     + brief    any harness
 silently     wiki pages       injection

Agents emit sanitized observations through lifecycle hooks as you work. At session end, observations become coherent markdown pages in the project's wiki (optionally LLM-written; useful even without). The next session, in any agent on any machine, gets a bounded brief and can search everything: full-text, entities, links, and (optionally) vectors, fused into one ranking. Cross-agent handoffs pass the baton explicitly.

The full design, including the invariants that keep multi-user and multi-session use safe, is in .

An optional server-rendered management console provides user administration, session inspection and deletion, and personal MCP API keys. Build with and start serve --transport http --enable-management-ui; both compile-time and runtime opt-ins are required.

Every row below is a first-party integration (MCP registration, lifecycle hooks, or both) checked by CI. The full matrix with per-agent notes and caveats is in .

OpenCode (V1/V2 auto-detected)
OpenCode V2 compatibility aliases (, , )

Coming from another tool?

Most agent-memory tools optimize for one thing: extracting atomic facts per turn, a temporal knowledge graph, an agent-editable memory OS, or a hosted context API. ai-memory is built around a git-backed markdown wiki as the source of truth, with a derived index for retrieval. It captures automatically from lifecycle hooks, is shared across agents, machines, and people, and works with zero LLM calls by default. This table shows what carries over from each tool and what you gain:

(LangMem)Automatic per-turn captureMemory compiles into readable you own and edit, not opaque fact rows; retrieval fuses FTS + entity + graph (+ local vectors) with no cloud API key
(temporal KG)Temporal reasoning, typed relationsBi-temporal-lite (, version-filtered search) and typed edges without standing up a graph database, in one binary
(fact rows, SQLite)SQLite + local embeddings, hook capture, typed edges, honest numbers, and, on 2.4, per-tier decay curves, extractive compression, DBSCAN cold-cluster dedup, access reinforcement, and contradiction flaggingHuman-editable markdown instead of fact-rows, cross-agent claim-once handoffs, and the same aging machinery done zero-LLM by default, reversibly (supersede-not-delete + ), and
(file-first markdown)Markdown-on-disk as the source of truthAutomatic lifecycle capture and a derived FTS/entity/graph index on top, cross-agent handoffs, and multi-user sharing built in
Claude Code built-in memory"Remember my project" convenience, zero setupSynced across machines and agents, searchable, team-capable, and captures tool lifecycle, unlike a per-laptop
(LLM or VLM in the loop)Living pages / document memory with a background consolidation loop, plus, on 2.4, belief-strength confidence plus an opt-in LLM "dream" rewrite of cold clustersA self-contained binary that runs zero-LLM by default and keeps memory in markdown files that are the source of truth, not a mirror; claim-once handoffs; the dream/belief features are opt-in, off by default, and never delete a source (vs a mandatory LLM loop)
(hosted memory API)A managed second brain with automatic ingestionGit-versioned markdown you own, no required API spend, offline operation, and per-project team sharing; ai-memory remembers , not a general vault

Across all of these, ai-memory gives you files you own (git-backed markdown), a zero-LLM default, one self-contained binary, sharing across agents, machines, and teams, automatic lifecycle capture, and typed, claim-once handoffs. Opt-in features (LLM consolidation, vector search, the "dream" consolidation pass, belief-strength in ranking) stay opt-in, and the zero-LLM aging path (per-tier decay, extractive compaction, dedup, contradiction flagging, access-weighted retention) works with no API key at all.

The full comparison, covering where each approach wins, where ai-memory differs, and the published benchmark, is in How ai-memory compares.

Linux and macOS (two commands, no root)

curl -fsSL https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
ai-memory setup

downloads the release for your OS and CPU, checks it against the release's published SHA-256 checksum (it refuses to install without a match), and links . then creates the data directory with a bearer token in an owner-only file, starts a per-user service (systemd or a launchd LaunchAgent), and wires MCP, hooks and Agent Skills for every agent it finds, or the ones you name with . It shows the plan, with where it found each agent, and asks first: answer , or type the numbers of the agents to wire. prints the plan and changes nothing, shows the plan as a page in your browser and applies the agents you tick there, skips the question, and running it again changes nothing. Afterwards, restart your agents and ask one of them "What do you remember about this project?" to see it answer through ai-memory. Details, the environment variables and how to verify the script before running it are in . An AI agent installing ai-memory for you can follow .

Claude Code and Codex users can wire their agent as a marketplace plugin instead (the binary is still installed as above):

claude plugin marketplace add akitaonrails/ai-memory && claude plugin install ai-memory@ai-memory
codex plugin marketplace add akitaonrails/ai-memory && codex plugin add ai-memory@ai-memory

Windows (two commands, no admin)

irm https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex
ai-memory setup

checks the release zip against its published SHA-256 checksum, unpacks it under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\ai-memory and adds that directory to your user . then does what it does on Linux and macOS, with a logon entry in place of the service: the server starts when you sign in, with no console window, and restarts if it fails. Details and the other Windows setups (WSL2, Docker Desktop, a real Windows service) are in .

For native Arch installs, use the AUR packages. They install , packaged hook sources, and both system-level and user-level systemd units.

yay -S ai-memory-bin    # prebuilt Linux x86_64/aarch64 binary
yay -S ai-memory        # builds from source
ai-memory setup         # data dir, user service, agents, self-check

Download the or RPM from the latest release, then install it:

sudo dnf install ./ai-memory-*.rpm

On a single-user workstation, then does the rest, as on the two-command path above: data dir and token, a user service, the agents it finds, and a self-check.

A self-contained that bundles the native binary and tree, starts the existing LaunchAgent, and opens , , and from the menu bar. Wiki, SQLite, config, and models stay in ~/Library/Application Support/ai-memory, so replacing the app is an update and does not rewrite that tree.

Needs a Rust toolchain and Xcode / Swift 6 (same as a source build):

git clone https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory
cd ai-memory
./companions/ai-memory-macos/build.sh
open "companions/ai-memory-macos/dist/AI Memory.app"

Drag to , then from the menu extra (no Dock icon). The app reads the bearer token wrote into its data dir, so the status item turns green on its own. Then wire your agents with the bundled binary; leaves the app's LaunchAgent in charge:

BIN="/Applications/AI Memory.app/Contents/Resources/runtime/ai-memory"
"$BIN" setup --no-service

You need: Docker or Podman + an agent CLI from the Support Matrix, or anything else that speaks MCP.

The published Docker image includes and variants, so Apple Silicon Macs and ARM64 Linux hosts can pull without emulation.

The Docker quick-start below has : the container never runs , so it starts without a token. The server binds to loopback only, so nothing outside the machine can reach it, but local processes and browser pages can. Native installs that run get a bearer token by default; see Security below for that and for adding a token here.

# 1. Install the ai-memory CLI wrapper (a small shell script that
#    runs the binary inside a container with your $HOME mounted). This is
#    the only thing that needs to live on the host filesystem.
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
wrapper_tmp="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$wrapper_tmp"' EXIT
wrapper_base=https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory/releases/latest/download/ai-memory-wrapper
curl -fsSL "$wrapper_base" -o "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper"
curl -fsSL "$wrapper_base.sha256" -o "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper.sha256"
expected="$(awk 'NR == 1 { print $1 }' "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper.sha256")"
if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    actual="$(sha256sum "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper" | awk '{ print $1 }')"
else
    actual="$(shasum -a 256 "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper" | awk '{ print $1 }')"
fi
[ -n "$expected" ] && [ "$actual" = "$expected" ] || { echo "wrapper checksum mismatch" >&2; exit 1; }
install -m 0755 "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper" ~/.local/bin/ai-memory
rm -rf "$wrapper_tmp"
trap - EXIT
# Most distros put ~/.local/bin on PATH automatically. If `which
# ai-memory` comes up empty, add this to ~/.bashrc / ~/.zshrc:
#     export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

# 2. Start the server. `--restart unless-stopped` makes it come back
#    on docker daemon restart and on machine boot (provided your
#    docker service is enabled at boot — `sudo systemctl enable
#    docker` on most distros). Loopback-only bind (`127.0.0.1:49374`)
#    so nothing outside this machine can reach it. Omit the LLM /
#    EMBEDDING lines for zero-LLM mode — FTS5 search still works
#    without any keys.
docker run -d --name ai-memory \
    --restart unless-stopped \
    -p 127.0.0.1:49374:49374 \
    -v ai-memory-data:/data \
    -e AI_MEMORY_LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic \
    -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... \
    -e AI_MEMORY_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=openai \
    -e OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... \
    docker.io/akitaonrails/ai-memory:latest

# 3. Wire your agent CLI in two commands. The wrapper takes care of
#    mounts and each client's config-path detection. Re-run with
#    `--agent codex`, `--agent command-code`, `--agent devin`, `--agent opencode`, `--agent opencode2`, `--agent gemini-cli`,
#    `--agent grok`, `--agent kimi-code`, `--agent kiro-cli`, `--agent copilot-cli`, `--agent droid`, `--agent muse`, `--agent cline`, `--agent qwen-code`, `--agent omp`,
#    `--agent oh-my-pi`, `--client cursor`,
#    `--client gemini-cli`, `--client grok`, `--client kiro-cli`,
#    `--client cline`, `--client freebuff`, etc.
#    for additional agents; full list in docs/install.md.
ai-memory install-mcp   --client claude-code --apply
ai-memory install-hooks --agent  claude-code --apply

On Linux and macOS, the Docker wrapper runs through its checksum-verified native host client. The installed hooks therefore enforce client-side capture controls such as and allowlist mode before an event reaches the spool or network. Set AI_MEMORY_HOOK_PLATFORM=posix explicitly only when you need the legacy shell compatibility path; the installer warns that path cannot enforce capture policy v1.

The examples use ; replace it with on a Podman host. The wrapper automatically uses Podman when Docker is not installed. Set to force Podman when both engines are available.

That completes the setup on Linux/macOS. Start a Claude Code session as usual: every prompt and tool call now lands in ai-memory, and the next session you open in this project will see a handoff with where you left off. On macOS the native binary is the recommended path when you do not need Docker, either through the menu bar app above or a release tarball / launchd agent. Later updates for that path use (checksum-verified GitHub release replace + hook refresh); see docs/install.md#keeping-ai-memory-up-to-date. The same native upgrade path covers Windows x86_64 zip installs under a writable prefix (see Scenario C). Upgrading a 2.x install of any kind to 3.0? Read first.

Wiring another agent is the same two commands with a different name: , , and so on for every row of the support matrix. OpenCode is version-detected by host-side commands; when generating its artifacts inside a container, use setup-agent --agent opencode --opencode-dialect v1|v2 --to /tmp/unused because the container cannot inspect the host executable. The aliases remain force-V2 compatibility spellings. The full per-agent guide, including Windows and remote servers, is .

Two agents in the same project at once, or teammates on one server, work out of the box: the "current project" pointer is isolated per caller by default (v1.39+). See for the optional session-aware Claude Code bridge and the details.

If in doubt, start your harness with . It is the preferred way to launch: the first time it runs a harness it auto-installs that harness's ai-memory hooks + MCP if they are missing (so capture and recall work without a separate / step to forget), it wires the right project scope by construction, and it adds cross-harness continuity on top of shared memory. Everything is idempotent and one-time per harness and config home. If the server is unreachable, warns and launches anyway with local capture spooling; run after the server returns (see Degraded offline launches). Pass to fail closed instead.

ai-memory run claude
ai-memory run codex --yolo   # same workstream + local Claude history dossier
ai-memory run --profile work claude  # reusable config.toml env/account preset
ai-memory continue           # resume the newest managed checkout
# after a dead launcher left its lease behind (same operator only)
ai-memory run --force-unlock codex
ai-memory resume             # pick from ALL workstreams in this checkout only
ai-memory resume --search auth # find a workstream by name (case-insensitive)
ai-memory resume --all       # pick across every linked checkout

immediately expires the selected workstream's active lease; use it only when you know the previous launcher is gone. It does not kill a native process, and it cannot evict another authenticated operator's run. See the managed-workstream recovery notes for the full safety contract.

On a real harness switch, the receiving managed agent is told to consult AI_MEMORY_PREVIOUS_SESSION_HISTORY when you ask to continue and the bounded portable packet lacks a detail. The variable names a private temporary Markdown projection created from the previous harness's checkout-validated, read-only adapter; the file disappears when the managed child exits. It is local to the launcher machine. This covers quota exhaustion and other abrupt exits where the old harness cannot write a handoff: refreshed ai-memory routing also tells the new agent that "continue", "resume", and "pick up where we left off" mean to read that file first when the three managed-run variables are present. A switch on another machine still gets the server's portable ledger and handoff, but cannot read a native transcript that exists only on the first machine.

Without the managed launcher, a harness cut off the same way leaves no handoff at all, so the next one could pick up an older handoff or session page. When the newest captured work in the project is in another of your sessions that never ended and left no handoff after that work, the next session start carries a one-line notice that names that session. The agent then reads its newest prompts and tool results with memory_read_session_observations. The same session is listed first in 's , and names it as .

If that variable is absent on a real same-machine switch, run and in the launching shell. This path requires the 3.1.0 or newer host client; a stale Cargo or package-manager binary earlier in can shadow an updated wrapper.

In , type to search, use Up/Down to select a workstream, and Left/Right to choose its harness. Enter launches the selection; Escape clears a search, then cancels when the search is empty (Ctrl-C always cancels). The list scrolls and loads every checkout-local page; there is no default workstream cutoff. Use only when you want to cap the matching results. Workstreams from other repositories or worktrees are left out unless you pass , which lists every linked checkout (the current one first); still resumes the newest linked checkout from anywhere. Listing reads Git identity only; it does not scan the working tree with before showing the picker. Full checkpoints are still captured when launching the selected workstream.

Auto-wiring is on by default; opt out with ai-memory run --no-autowire or AI_MEMORY_RUN_AUTOWIRE=false. You can still wire agents by hand with / (e.g. for a harness you never launch through ).

ai-memory uninstall --apply removes everything ai-memory installed, and only what it installed. It also clears 's auto-wire record, so the next managed launch wires that harness again; to keep it unwired, launch with or set AI_MEMORY_RUN_AUTOWIRE=false. Install commands are idempotent and write timestamped backups next to any file they touch.

This flake ships a NixOS module () with a systemd.services.ai-memory unit: a dedicated system user (, no linger) plus a hardened systemd sandbox (, empty capability sets, , , and the rest; see ). Packaged FHS units under keep their existing lighter hardening. The flake exports packages for , , and . Intel macOS remains supported by the release tarball and Homebrew, but not by the pinned Nixpkgs revision.

{
  inputs.ai-memory.url = "github:akitaonrails/ai-memory";

  outputs = { nixpkgs, ai-memory, ... }: {
    nixosConfigurations.myhost = nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem {
      system = "x86_64-linux";
      modules = [
        ai-memory.nixosModules.default
        {
          services.ai-memory = {
            enable = true;
            # enableWeb = true;  # off by default — the web UI is opt-in
            # enableApi = true;  # API-only companions; no browser UI
            settings = {
              allowed_hosts = [ "localhost" "127.0.0.1" "::1" "homelab.example" ];
              log_level = "info";
            };
            # Loopback (default): secrets optional; missing env file is tolerated.
            # Non-loopback: set one of ageSecret, sopsSecret, or environmentFile.
            # ageSecret = "ai-memory-env";  # config.age.secrets.<name> (agenix)
            # sopsSecret = "ai-memory/env"; # config.sops.secrets.<name> (sops-nix)
          };
        }
      ];
    };
  };
}

Declarative non-secret config lives in services.ai-memory.settings (a small typed set for common keys, plus for the rest of ). The module renders a generated TOML file and passes . Top-level , , and win over duplicate settings keys. Anything in (including ) lands in a world-readable Nix store path, so do not put API keys there.

Secrets such as never go in or the world-readable Nix store. This includes , which can carry API credentials; set in , , or instead. These three secret sources are mutually exclusive. Non-loopback binds require one; loopback may omit them and tolerates a missing environment file (systemd ). Put TLS in front of a LAN/WAN bind; see .

All options and defaults are in . The module is entirely opt-in: , , , and the CLI are unchanged if you don't import it.

is a runtime dependency. Hook capture and run it to read the repository a session works in. The module puts on the service's . The package itself leaves the binary unwrapped, because a wrapper renames the running process and the live-process guard in , , and looks for a process named . If you install the package without the module (, ), install next to it.

Day to day, you mostly do not think about ai-memory. Hooks capture prompts, tool calls, and session boundaries; session end turns them into readable wiki pages; the next session starts with a handoff.

  • Ask "where did we leave off?" to continue from the pending handoff.
  • Import a local PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, Markdown file, or VTT/SRT transcript as attributed, sanitized memory with the optional command.
  • Ask "have we discussed X?" or "search memory for Y" to query the wiki.
  • Narrow a large wiki before ranking with filters such as path_prefix: "procedures/", , , or .
  • Inspect content-free per-workload LLM call, outcome, latency, and usage telemetry with ; it diagnoses the configured provider but does not route different workloads to different models.
  • Ask "catch me up" for a prose digest of recent project activity, or run ( for every project) to list the newest pages.
  • Search Chinese, Japanese and Korean text without spaces: zero-LLM search matches unspaced Han, Kana and Hangul substrings.
  • Run once when adopting an existing project with months of history.
  • Start the server with for a read-only browser view of the wiki, a link graph at , a root/operator managed-workstream overview at , and a JSON API under . On a server with a bearer token and no user accounts (every fresh install), the browser asks for a username and password: any username, and the contents of <data_dir>/auth-tokens/default as the password.
  • Back up host-side harness configuration with ai-memory backup-agents -o agent-assets.tar.gz; inspect a restore with ai-memory restore-agents -i agent-assets.tar.gz, then add only after reviewing the active skills, plugins, instructions, and destinations.

Teams and multiple machines

Run the server somewhere reachable, such as a homelab box or a LAN host, and point every machine and every teammate at it. Knowledge is shared per project; personal handoffs stay personal; every write is attributed and audited. Multi-user auth (passwords, API credentials) is built in.

Start with for accounts and ownership, and for the server itself. It includes measured capacity numbers and the one rule you must follow: one server per data directory, never two.

Two opt-in HTTP surfaces build on the same browser sign-in, and both are off by default. serve --enable-session-management lets signed-in users inspect sessions and purge the ones they own (docs/session-management.md). serve --enable-self-service-keys lets them issue and revoke their own API keys (docs/self-service-keys.md).

The server binds to loopback only by default. A fresh also mints a root bearer token into the data dir, which the hooks, the CLI and the stdio bridge read from there; it is never written into a harness config. An install created before that default (and the Docker quick-start) runs without auth until , and says so. From there, hardening is incremental: a bearer token for the LAN, per-user accounts, OIDC device auth for hooks, TLS via a reverse proxy. Capture is sanitized at a typed privacy boundary before anything is stored, and per-repository rules can exclude paths or invert to allowlist mode. A repository can also route its capture to a different server than the one the hooks were installed against. Human login beyond loopback requires an HTTPS posture by default. Operators who explicitly accept plaintext passwords, cookies, credentials, and memory traffic on a private LAN can opt in with serve --allow-insecure-human-auth; the server never enables that exception implicitly.

Optional. Everything works with zero LLM calls; adding a provider upgrades session summaries and enables semantic search. Anthropic, OpenAI (including OAuth), Codex CLI credential reuse, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, OpenCode (Go and Zen), the Cursor Agent CLI (), and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM) are supported for consolidation; OpenAI, Voyage, Gemini, and keyless OpenAI-compatible endpoints for embeddings. Configuration lives in .

One Rust binary runs an MCP/HTTP server and owns one data directory:

<data_dir>/
├── wiki/    # markdown source of truth, git-versioned
├── raw/     # immutable sanitized managed-workstream transcript segments
├── db/      # SQLite indexes, including FTS5, entities, and embeddings
├── models/  # reserved for local embedding models
└── logs/    # rolling tracing output

Hooks POST observations to the server. The server serializes writes through one SQLite writer, compiles session observations into markdown pages, and serves retrieval through FTS5, entity-match and graph-neighbor RRF, optional vector RRF, an observation-evidence stream that lifts a session's page when its captured turns match (on by default), bounded source-authority adjustment, and bounded raw-observation fallback for non-global searches.

Task-oriented cheat sheet. "I want to do X" → how: recall prior work, keep a project rule, import an existing knowledge base, get two agents/repos working together. Start here.
Every agent CLI, every alternative (curl, source build, no-docker, no-auth), and the server-on-a-different-machine walkthrough.
Handoffs, proactive memory queries, slim routing snippet + managed Agent Skills, web UI, raw-wiki inspection, and the rules, memory and profile precedence.
The cross-project profile. Your usual choices delivered to every project as defaults: defaults per deployment, every setting, per-project opt-outs, multi-user opt-in and privacy, CLI.
Optional continuity across harnesses: auto harness selection, native resume, argument forwarding, ledger search, privacy, and recovery.
Cross-project agent-to-agent messaging: a directed, claim-once inbox/queue plus the on-start "you have mail" notice.
Default repository-path project naming plus workspace/project routing for multi-client trees, mono-repos, worktrees, and work/personal separation, plus per-repository server profiles.
modes for shared servers: the default isolation, session-aware isolation, and the pre-v1.39 slot.
macOS install paths: menu bar app, native release tarball, source build, Docker wrapper, launchd, and current limitations.
Windows install modes: full WSL2, native Windows with Docker Desktop, prebuilt native release zip, native source builds, and caveats.
Per-client MCP and lifecycle notes, handoff-injection limits, and community bridge guidance.
Homelab deploy: bin/deploy, bearer-token auth, pointers to the TLS guide.
Multi-user attribution and human login. Four-rung bearer ladder, password sessions, / walkthrough, brownfield migration.
Optional server-rendered console: feature gates, user and session management, MCP keys, public deployment, and frontend checks.
HTTPS via a reverse proxy. When you need TLS and when you don't, with copy-paste Caddy / nginx / Cloudflare Tunnel templates and the "secure when you're not" failure modes.
Read before purge / rename / backup / restore / reset / reindex / restore-page. Safety matrix, per-project disk layout, checkpoint page recovery, and operator workflows.
Backing up the wiki + data dir to a remote git repository: what to include, what to exclude, scheduled push pattern, restore, and security posture. Companion to (which covers the on-box snapshot).
Host agent-asset backup/restore: supported paths, filtering, redaction limits, archive bounds, active-content warning, and rollback behavior.
Data-flow reference for security/legal review. What's stored, what's local-only, the two opt-in external paths, and how deletion/retention work.
Enterprise identity: the OIDC device-auth flow, its scope, and how to front the server with an OIDC-aware gateway.
Offline/air-gapped install: self-contained build, checksum-verified release binaries, and offline local embedding models.
Upgrading a 2.x install to 3.0: what changed, the removed token commands and their replacements, upgrade steps, and rollback.
Upgrading an existing store to 2.0: the backup-gated automatic migration and how to restore.
Published retrieval-quality numbers with provenance, reproducible from the in-repo harness.
The wiki is natively an Open Knowledge Format (OKF v0.2) bundle; design and field mapping.

Dated , , , , and files are evidence and design records, not current operating instructions. Their status or snapshot banner says whether work shipped, remains proposed, or has been superseded. Use the user guides and for current behavior; the older records remain only when current design rationale links to them.

Written by users; not maintained here, so check them against the version you run.

This codebase is being built collaboratively with Claude Code (Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7) following the plan documented in .

items.title: MadsLorentzen/ai-job-search
items.content:
The job search that runs on your machine. AI job application framework built on Claude Code: evaluate postings, tailor CVs, write cover letters, prep interviews. Fork it and own it.

The job search that runs on your machine.

An AI-powered job application framework built on Claude Code. Fork it, fill in your profile, and let Claude evaluate job postings, tailor your CV, write cover letters, and prepare you for interviews.

Note: This is an independent open-source project and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, sponsored by, or maintained by Anthropic. Anthropic and Claude Code are referenced only to describe the toolchain this workflow uses.

This project has no affiliated cryptocurrency, token, or paid sponsorship program. Anything claiming otherwise is unauthorized and should be treated as a scam. The only ways to support the project are the Ko-fi link below and contributing on GitHub.

I'm a geophysicist by training. When my position was cut in late 2025, I built this framework to run my own job search - the same , , and workflow in this repo, used weekly, on my own career. I was upfront about it with every employer I spoke to, and instead of counting against me, it usually sparked a genuine technical conversation.

Sixty-nine tailored applications, twenty first interviews, and one signed contract later, I started as an AI engineer in June 2026. People kept asking whether this actually works. It got me hired. Now it's yours.

The longer version, including the full application funnel, is on LinkedIn.

Did this save you a Sunday of cover-letter writing? Consider a coffee. Did it land you the job? Maybe two. ☕

A structured workflow that turns Claude Code into a full-stack job application assistant. The core workflow (self-profiling, fit evaluation, and the drafter-reviewer application pipeline) is language- and country-agnostic. The job portal search skills are built for the Danish market (Jobindex, Jobnet, Akademikernes Jobbank, etc.), but the pattern is designed to be swapped for your local job boards.

/setup          /scrape              /apply <url>
  |                |                     |
  v                v                     v
Fill in        Search job           Evaluate fit
your profile   portals              Score & recommend
  |                |                     |
  v                v                     v
Profile        Present matches      Draft CV + Cover Letter
files ready    with fit ratings     (LaTeX, tailored)
                   |                     |
                   v                     v
               Pick a match         Reviewer agent critiques
               -> /apply            -> Revise -> Final output

The framework encodes career guidance best practices, including structured evaluation criteria, forward-looking cover letter framing, and optional salary benchmarking.

  • Claude Code (CLI). Claude Code has no free tier: you need a Claude Pro/Max/Team subscription or Anthropic API credits (pay-per-token, usually cheaper for occasional use). Using a different agent tool (Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI)? Start at - the portal search skills work there out of the box, and community forks adapt the full workflow.
  • Bun (for job search CLI tools)
  • LaTeX distribution with and : TeX Live, MacTeX, TinyTeX, or MiKTeX. The CV compiles with (pdflatex often fails on modern MiKTeX installs with font-expansion errors); the cover letter compiles with because requires . If using a minimal TeX install such as TinyTeX or BasicTeX, install the extra packages listed in SETUP.md.
  • Optional: for 's ATS parseability check (BSD; no Poppler required). Poppler remains a fallback (macOS: , Debian/Ubuntu: apt install poppler-utils, Windows: ). If both are missing, the check degrades to a visual keyword review.
gh repo fork MadsLorentzen/ai-job-search --clone
cd ai-job-search

A fork of this repo is always public — GitHub does not allow private forks of public repositories — and (step 3 below) writes your personal data (name, contact details, employment history, salary expectations) into files. If this copy is for your own job search rather than for contributing changes back, use a with this repo as instead — the two-minute recipe is in SETUP.md section 8, and every update workflow works identically. Fork only to contribute.

2. Install job search tools

python3 tools/install_portal_clis.py   # Windows: python tools\install_portal_clis.py

It runs in every portal CLI under - discovered, not listed, so a portal you add with or copy from another fork is included on a fresh clone. A CLI whose declares an install-time lifecycle script is skipped and reported rather than run. shows what it would install.

For and the install is optional: both have zero runtime dependencies and run with plain ; only pulls TypeScript dev types.

claude
# Then inside Claude Code:
/setup

offers three paths: read your folder if you have one populated (CV PDF, LinkedIn export, diplomas, reference letters, past applications), import a single CV pasted in chat, or walk through an interview. It auto-detects what you have and asks. Documents-folder mode is idempotent and safe to re-run as you add more material; see for the layout.

This searches multiple job portals for positions matching your profile, deduplicates results, and presents them sorted by fit. Pick a match to run on it directly — or, when a scrape returns more jobs than you want to eyeball, run to batch-score them all against the fit framework and get a ranked shortlist first.

/apply https://jobindex.dk/job/1234567

If the URL can't be fetched (some job portals block automated access), you can paste the job description directly instead:

/apply <paste the full job description here>

This runs the full workflow: evaluate fit, draft CV + cover letter, review with a second agent, revise, and present the final output. The posting passes a deterministic integrity gate first (hidden text, invisible characters, instruction-shaped lines, hidden links), and its one-line verdict opens the evaluation; the agents that fetch and review read-only.

Postings are treated as untrusted input (the workflow follows no instructions embedded in them and fetches no links from their body), but agentic defenses are instruction-level, not a sandbox - on an unfamiliar job board, skim what was fetched and written before you hit send. Details in SECURITY.md.

, , and form the core workflow. Ten more commands extend it once your profile is in place:

  • preps you for a scheduled interview on a tracked application. It builds a stage-specific prep pack from the application's archive (the exact posting, the CV and cover letter the interviewer actually read, feedback recorded from earlier rounds), researches the company and interviewers with a verify-before-use rule, maps likely questions to your STAR examples, and offers a mock interview following the roleplay protocol in . Gaps get honest bridge answers, never invented experience.
  • records what happened to an application - interview stages, offers, rejections, silence. It archives the submitted CV, cover letter, and posting text into documents/applications/<company>_<role>/, keeps in the format Path A parses, and updates the tracker. It also owns the stretch before there is an outcome to record: surfaces open applications that have gone quiet (default 10 days), drafts a short channel-appropriate follow-up in your writing style using only claims from the materials you already submitted (drafts only, never sends; at most twice per application), and offers a thank-you note in the same turn an interview stage is recorded. Once a few applications resolve, it points you back to to calibrate the fit framework from what actually got interviews.
  • publishes a one-way, read-only view of the pipeline into a Notion database via the official Notion MCP server (OAuth, no API keys) - one row per ranked job plus every tracked application, with a write-once briefing page per row. The repo files stay the system of record: nothing syncs back, and documents sync as filenames only. Complements : that is the deep offline dashboard you regenerate at your desk; this is the glanceable live view from anywhere Notion runs (desktop, web, phone).
  • reads your Gmail (via the Gmail connector) for status signals on your open applications - interview invites, assessment links, offers, rejections - and proposes them as a batch for you to approve before anything is written to the tracker or , citing the source email on every proposed change. Offers stop short of proposing / since that's your call; conflicting or unmatched signals get flagged for a manual pass instead of guessed.
  • bridges and : it batch-scores all newly scraped postings against the fit framework (parallel agents fetch each posting and score the five evaluation dimensions) and returns a ranked shortlist with honest per-job strengths and gaps. Deal-breakers veto, deadlines get urgency flags, dead postings get marked expired. Pick a number and it hands off to the full workflow.
  • enriches your profile by scanning public sources you've already linked in it (GitHub repos, portfolio site, Kaggle, Google Scholar) and looking up syllabi for named courses and certifications. Discovered competencies are added to your profile with a source tag. Useful right after to surface skills that documents alone don't make explicit.
  • analyzes the gap between your profile, your tracked job postings, and your ranked-but-untracked postings ('s recorded gaps in job_scraper/seen_jobs.json) — or a single posting via . Produces a prioritized heatmap of skill gaps and a learning plan with web-searched study resources and time estimates. Useful for career planning between applications.
  • generates a self-contained HTML dashboard from and the application archives — stat cards, status/sector/channel/funnel charts (inline SVG, no external dependencies), and a filterable applications table. Opens directly in a browser, fully offline. Re-run it any time after or adds new entries.
  • registers your own CV or cover letter template (LaTeX, Typst, or another toolchain) in place of the stock ones. It captures the template's instructions (source extension, compile command, fonts, style rules, page limit), runs a mandatory test compile, and wires the template into . See Custom templates below.
  • generates a job-portal search skill for a job board in your market. It investigates the portal (search URL pattern, result structure, access rules), scaffolds the CLI skill from the same structure as the shipped ones, and test-runs a live query before registering. See Job search tools below.

│   ├── posting_guard.py               # Integrity gate: strip hidden text, flag injection-shaped lines

│   ├── security_guards.py             # CI guards: permission allow/ask/deny, skill grants, gitignore, manifests

│   ├── verify_layout.py               # Measure a compiled PDF's page layout (holes, orphans, footer collisions)
│   ├── verify_pdf.py                  # Verify a compiled PDF's page count and extractable text
│   └── README_SALARY_TOOL.md          # Salary tool setup instructions
